title: Too much to trust: how conflicting and misleading health information shape patient trust and social media behavior
screen_reason: Secondary analysis of HINTS Cycle 6 (US, March-November 2022). The paper's aim is a PLS-SEM model of trust, but Appendix Table 5 prints the full response distribution for the HINTS misinformation item - 'How much of the health information that you see on social media do you think is false or misleading?' - as counts and percentages (None 1.58%, A little 17.50%, Some 46.80%, A lot 34.12%). Perceived amount of misinformation in one's environment reported as a share of respondents is an eligible RECALL (exposure) estimate.

estimates.country: United States (Health Information National Trends Survey, National Cancer Institute)
estimates.platform: Social media (platform unspecified in the item; respondents restricted to social media users)
estimates.date: March to November 2022 (HINTS Cycle 6 field period)
estimates.measure_type: % of US adult social media users who say 'a lot' of the health information they see on social media is false or misleading
estimates.denominator: 4,314 respondents who answered the item (analytic sample of 4,594 US adults who had accessed social media at least a few times in the past 12 months, drawn from 6,252 HINTS 6 respondents; non-users coded missing)
estimates.definition: Respondent selected the top category 'A lot' when asked how much of the health information they see on social media they think is false or misleading
estimates.misinfo_def: "unintentionally false or misleading content shared without malicious intent" (paper's definition); the item itself asks about health information that is "false or misleading"
estimates.source_quote: How much of the health information that you see on social media do you think is false or misleading? None 68 (1.58%) Alittle 755 (17.50%) Some 2019 (46.80%) Alot 1472 (34.12%)
estimates.page_loc: Appendix, Table 5 'Constructs, measures, and descriptive statistics'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Respondents' own perception of the health information they encounter; single HINTS item taken from Stimpson and Ortega (2023); no external verification of any content. Respondents answering 'I do not use social media' were coded as missing.
estimates.moderator_quote: Misinformation on social media was assessed by the following survey question (Stimpson and Ortega 2023): “How much of the health information that you see on social media do you think is false or misleading?” The response categories were: “I do not use social media”, “None”, “A little”, “Some”, and “A lot”. Those reporting that they do not use social media were coded as missing. | Hypotheses in this study were tested with data from the Health Information National Trends Survey (HINTS) Cycle 6, administered by the National Cancer Institute (NCI) between March and November 2022. ... a total response of 6,252 participants. ... we refined our dataset to include only participants who had accessed social media at least a few times within the past 12 months ... the finalized dataset included 4,594 individuals.
estimates.notes: Denominator is 4,314 (the four printed cells sum to 4,314 and each percentage reproduces exactly: 1472/4314 = 34.12%, 2019/4314 = 46.80%), i.e. 280 of the 4,594 analytic cases did not answer the item. Note the sample is social media USERS, not all US adults, so the base is narrower than a general-population estimate. Only the verbatim 'A lot' cell is kept: the more commonly quoted 'some or a lot' figure (80.92%) and 'any misinformation' (98.42%) would be cross-category sums, forbidden by R8, and 100 - 1.58 would be a computed complement. platform_norm coded multi_platform because the item names social media generically rather than one platform.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) The other printed cells of the same item (None 1.58%, A little 17.50%, Some 46.80%) are available but are middle/complement categories rather than a threshold share; only the top category was taken as the row, per R4/R8. An adjudicator wanting a 'some or a lot' figure should note it would be a computed sum (80.92%). 2) Conflicting-health-information items ('How often do health recommendations from experts seem to change over time?' Often 59.88%, Very Often 12.44%; 'conflict or contradict one another?' Often 48.31%, Very Often 8.65%) are about expert disagreement, not misinformation, and were not extracted. 3) Behavioural shares reported in the sample description - 26.75% talked to people with similar issues on social media, 68.02% watched health-related videos, 38.29% shared general health information - are health social-media use, not misinformation exposure or misinformation sharing, so not eligible. 4) The Introduction cites 'roughly 15-30% of health-related content on social media is misleading or false' (Suarez-Lledo and Alvarez-Galvez 2021) and 'some extreme cures accounting for over one-third of related content' (Kouzy et al. 2020) - figures taken from elsewhere, excluded by R8. 5) All model results (beta coefficients, R2, inverted-U effects) are associations, not prevalence.

rob.design: Secondary cross-sectional analysis of the Health Information National Trends Survey (HINTS) Cycle 6, a nationally recognised probability survey of US adults administered by the National Cancer Institute by paper and online between March and November 2022; 6,252 total respondents. The authors screened out non-users and infrequent social media users (kept those who accessed social media at least a few times in the past 12 months) plus outliers, missing values and error responses, leaving 4,594; the misinformation item has 4,314 valid answers. Misinformation and trust-in-doctors are SINGLE items (the authors themselves flag this as a limitation and note the trust measure is cancer-specific); PCC (7 items), conflicting information (2 items) and social media health behaviour (3 items) are multi-item with Cronbach's alpha > 0.70, CR > 0.70, AVE > 0.50, Fornell-Larcker discriminant validity met, VIF 1.00-3.39. Common-method variance checked by Harman's single factor (20.6%) and a marker variable (Smoke100). Analysis by PLS-SEM (SmartPLS 4.0) with quadratic terms. No response rate, weighting or design-effect adjustment is reported in the text.
